t: Find the Count of Numbers Which Are Not Special
o: A number has exactly 2 proper divisors iff it is the square of a prime: proper divisors of p² are {1, p}. (p³ has {1,p,p²}, composites with ≥2 prime factors have more.) So special numbers in [l,r] are exactly squares of primes p with p² in range. Since r ≤ 1e9, p ≤ 31623; sieve primes up to 31623+ and count those whose square lands in [l,r]. Answer = (r−l+1) − count.
k: Special ⟺ p² for prime p: exactly the numbers with divisor count 3.
Sieve primes only up to ⌊√r⌋ ≈ 31623 (use 31700 to be safe).
Answer = range length minus the number of prime squares inside it.

a.n: Approach 1: Sieve of Eratosthenes up to sqrt(r)
a.i: Enumerate primes p ≤ √r via sieve; count p with l ≤ p² ≤ r; subtract from the interval length.
s: Sieve booleans up to N = floor(sqrt(r)) + 1.
For each prime p, if p*p >= l and p*p <= r, increment cnt.
a.t: O(√r log log √r) — sieving up to ~31623 dominates; the final scan is linear in that bound

a.n: Approach 2: Segmented counting without full sieve scan
a.i: Identical sieve, but count prime squares via a closed-form prime-counting comparison: iterate primes and test the range condition — same thing; alternatively precompute the prime list once and binary search squares. Complexity unchanged; useful if many queries arrive.
s: Sieve once and extract the prime list.
For a query [l, r], binary search primes with p² ≥ l and p² ≤ r.
Subtract the count from r − l + 1.
a.t: O(√r log log √r) — dominated by the sieve; per-query work is O(π(√r))

w: The entire difficulty is the number-theory reduction: exactly-two-proper-divisors ⟺ p². Double-check boundary handling (l = 1: 1 has zero proper divisors, not special; perfect squares of composites like 16 are not special). Use 64-bit for p*p to avoid overflow near 1e9. Follow-up: count special numbers directly, or handle r up to 1e18 with a segmented sieve over [⌊√l⌋, ⌈√r⌉].
